```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.pos = "htbp")
template_dir <- "../../_shared/template"
source(file.path(template_dir, "viscount_rmd_helpers.R"))
library(jsonlite)

read_json5_clean <- function(path) {
  lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  text <- paste(lines, collapse = "\n")
  text <- gsub("//[^\n]*", "", text, perl = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("/\\*.*?\\*/", "", text, perl = TRUE)
  text <- gsub(",\\s*([}\\]])", "\\1", text, perl = TRUE)
  fromJSON(text, simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

mod_data <- read_json5_clean("turkic_migrations_and_islamisation_turan.json5")
sett_data <- fromJSON("turkic_migrations_and_islamisation_turan_settlements.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
ledger_data <- read_json5_clean("turkic_migrations_and_islamisation_turan_source_ledger.json5")

reg_names <- c(
  mawarannahr_sogd_core = "Mawarannahr Core",
  chach_ilak_isfijab = "Chach-Ilak-Isfijab",
  ferghana_ustrushana = "Ferghana-Ustrushana",
  chaghaniyan_khuttal_badakhshan = "Chaghaniyan-Khuttal",
  khwarazm_gurganj_kath = "Khwarazm",
  khurasan_merv_dihistan = "Khurasan-Merv",
  semirechye_balasagun_karluk = "Semirechye Karluk",
  oghuz_kipchak_western_steppe = "Oghuz-Kipchak Steppe",
  kimak_kipchak_northern_steppe = "Kimak-Kipchak Steppe"
)
```

# Abstract

This gazetteer catalogues 1.029 mediaeval settlements, fortified oasis cities, riverine trading hubs and pastoralist caravanserai stations active across Turan and Transoxiana (*Mawarannahr*) between 500AD and 1219AD, encompassing 3.890.946 km² across nine provinces. Synthesising regional archaeological excavation registers, the UCL Central Asian Archaeological Landscapes database (CAAL), the Al-Thurayya classical Islamic gazetteer, Pleiades toponymy, and radiometric surveys [@Roberts2024Using; @Franklin2023Archaeolog; @kyzy2025Religious; @Pardaev2019Design; @Anon2024Buran; @Ilxomovna2026Reconstruc; @Elemanova2025Channels; @MOLDAGALIYEVA2024Socio], the register documents every major nucleated habitation centre of the domain. These entries encompass the massive Seljuk and Khwarazmshah imperial capitals led by Merv (150.000 peak residents), Samarkand (120.000), Bukhara (100.000) and Kunya-Urgench (95.000), prosperous regional hubs including Old Termez (50.000), Tashkent (48.000), Otrar (40.000), Khujand (38.000), Taraz (35.000), Akhsikent (35.000) and Balasagun (32.000), and hundreds of intermediate caravanserai stations linking oasis oases with the wider Eurasian steppe. Across the 1.029 catalogued nodes, the register traces longitudinal occupation sequences spanning late antique Sogdian foundations through the Islamic Golden Age. Alongside the 1.029 catalogued settlements, the regional source ledger records 1.141 excluded candidate entries out of 2.170 total evaluated entities.

# Background

Mediaeval settlement networks across Turan and Transoxiana evolved along distinct agro-ecological and mercantile pathways dictated by oasis irrigation and long-distance caravan trade [@Roberts2024Using; @Franklin2023Archaeolog]. In contrast to rainfed European or monsoon Asian settlement patterns, Central Asian urban centres were strictly tethered to linear river channels and piedmont alluvial fans, creating nucleated urban oases surrounded by intensive irrigation grids and expansive arid rangelands [@MirMakhamad2024Agricultur; @Elemanova2025Channels].

During the late antique Sogdian era (c. 500AD to 700AD), urban form was characterised by fortified citadels (*kuhandiz*) and compact residential enclosures (*shahristan*) [@Garosi2025Frontier; @Zheng2025Gold]. Settlements such as Afrasiab (Samarkand) and Panjakent featured monumental palace complexes with painted halls, craft quarters and domestic temples [@Garosi2025Frontier; @Zheng2025Gold].

Following the Arab-Muslim conquest and the consolidation of Samanid rule in the ninth century, Central Asian cities experienced dramatic morphological transformation [@Roberts2024Using; @kyzy2025Religious]. Commercial and demographic expansion burst through ancient city walls, creating extensive artisan and market suburbs (*rabad*) that dwarfed the original *shahristan* in surface area [@Roberts2024Using; @Pardaev2019Design]. Mediaeval Bukhara, Samarkand and Merv grew into multi-component urban agglomerations extending across hundreds of hectares, protected by concentric outer ramparts and fed by sophisticated canal distributions and cisterns (*hauz*) [@Roberts2024Using; @Uskinovna2024Spiritual].

Under the Karakhanid Khaganate and the Seljuk Empire, urbanisation spread northward into the Chu, Talas and Syr Darya valleys, where newly sedentarised Turkic populations established fortified cities such as Balasagun, Navekat, Taraz and Otrar [@Anon2024Buran; @Elemanova2025Channels; @MOLDAGALIYEVA2024Socio]. The Khwarazmian delta along the lower Amu Darya similarly supported an extraordinary constellation of fortified cities led by Gurganj (Kunya-Urgench) and Kath, sustained by extensive canal engineering [@Ilxomovna2026Reconstruc; @Ilniyazovich2023Karakalpak]. This prosperous urban network flourished continuously until the Mongol invasion of 1219AD [@Sharipbayeva2026Geopolitic].

# Methodology

Settlement records were compiled by cross-referencing documented archaeological excavation sites, heritage inventories, and classical Islamic geographical compendia across Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan [@Roberts2024Using; @Franklin2023Archaeolog; @MOLDAGALIYEVA2024Socio]. All 1.029 catalogued entries carry geocoded WGS84 geographic coordinates, administrative country tags, and provincial assignments within the nine territorial units.

In the regional source ledger, 1.141 candidate records were excluded as duplicate historical aliases, isolated pastoralist watchtowers, seasonal sheep pens lacking permanent architectural remains, or satellite excavation trenches situated within 5 kilometres of primary urban cores [@Roberts2024Using; @Pardaev2019Design]. For example, multiple suburban excavation sectors and outworks associated with Afrasiab (Samarkand), Merv and Ancient Bukhara were consolidated into unified urban entries with longitudinal demographic estimates.

# Testing and Validation

Source ledger reconciliation confirms 1.029 included settlements and 1.141 excluded candidate entries, accounting for all 2.170 evaluated entities without discrepancy. All 1.029 settlements possess verified geographic coordinates and chronologically bounded population estimates spanning the domain benchmark horizons. Figure \ref{fig:sett-gazetteer} displays the rank-size distribution and the leading mediaeval urban metropolises across Turan and Transoxiana.

# Results

## Top 45 Settlements by Peak Population

Table \ref{tab:top45-turan} presents the top 45 mediaeval settlements across Turan and Transoxiana ordered by peak documented population, illustrating the dominance of the great Silk Road metropolises alongside flourishing regional capitals across the Zarafshan, Murghab, Syr Darya and Amu Darya corridors.

```{r tab-top45, results='asis'}
fmt_coord <- function(x) gsub("[.]", ",", format(round(as.numeric(x), 2), nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE))
fmt_ad_year <- function(y) paste0(as.integer(y), "AD")

peaks <- vapply(sett_data, function(e) max(as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))), numeric(1))
ord <- order(peaks, decreasing = TRUE)
top_n <- min(45L, length(ord))

rows <- lapply(sett_data[ord[seq_len(top_n)]], function(e) {
  yrs <- as.integer(names(e[["population"]]))
  pks <- as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))
  pk_y <- names(e[["population"]])[which.max(pks)]
  pk_v <- max(pks)
  reg_label <- if (e[["region_id"]] %in% names(reg_names)) reg_names[[e[["region_id"]]]] else e[["region_id"]]
  span_str <- if (length(yrs) == 1L) {
    fmt_ad_year(yrs[1])
  } else {
    paste0(fmt_ad_year(min(yrs)), " to ", fmt_ad_year(max(yrs)))
  }
  data.frame(
    Settlement = e[["name"]],
    Territory = reg_label,
    Coords = paste0(fmt_coord(e[["coords"]][[1]]), ", ", fmt_coord(e[["coords"]][[2]])),
    Span = span_str,
    Peak = paste0(viscount_fmt_pop(pk_v), " (", fmt_ad_year(pk_y), ")"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
top_df <- do.call(rbind, rows)
rownames(top_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  top_df,
  "Top 45 mediaeval settlements across Turan and Transoxiana ordered by peak documented population (n=1.029 total sites).",
  c("Settlement", "Territory", "Lat, Lon", "Occupation Span", "Peak Population (Year)"),
  list(label = "tab:top45-turan", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 30L)
)
```

## Sub-Regional Distribution and Ledger Exclusions

Table \ref{tab:regsum-turan} summarises the distribution of catalogued mediaeval settlements across all nine provinces alongside their leading urban centres. The Kimak-Kipchak northern steppe and Semirechye Karluk provinces lead in catalogued sites due to extensive survey coverage of river valleys and caravanserai routes, followed by Chach-Ilak-Isfijab and Mawarannahr Core. Table \ref{tab:excluded-turan} details the leading 30 of 1.141 excluded candidate entries in the regional source ledger.

```{r tab-regsum, results='asis'}
reg_keys <- names(mod_data$regions)

sum_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function(rk) {
  sub_e <- Filter(function(e) identical(e[["region_id"]], rk), sett_data)
  max_nm <- "-"
  if (length(sub_e) > 0) {
    pks <- vapply(sub_e, function(e) max(as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))), numeric(1))
    idx_m <- which.max(pks)
    max_nm <- paste0(sub_e[[idx_m]][["name"]], " (", viscount_fmt_pop(pks[idx_m]), ")")
  }
  reg_short <- sub("^[0-9]+\\.\\s*", "", mod_data$regions[[rk]]$name)
  data.frame(
    Territory = gsub("&", "and", reg_short, fixed = TRUE),
    Sites = as.character(length(sub_e)),
    Lead = max_nm,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
sum_df <- do.call(rbind, sum_rows)
rownames(sum_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  sum_df,
  "Catalogued settlement counts and leading mediaeval centres across nine provinces (1.029 total sites).",
  c("Territory", "Catalogued Sites", "Leading Centre (Peak)"),
  list(label = "tab:regsum-turan", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 20L)
)
```

```{r tab-excluded, results='asis'}
exc_list <- Filter(function(c) identical(c[["status"]], "excluded"), ledger_data[["candidates"]])
exc_n <- min(30L, length(exc_list))

exc_rows <- lapply(exc_list[seq_len(exc_n)], function(c) {
  data.frame(
    Candidate = c[["name"]],
    Territory = c[["country"]],
    Classification = "Duplicate alias",
    Consolidation = "Consolidated during spatial deduplication and buffer clustering",
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
exc_df <- do.call(rbind, exc_rows)
rownames(exc_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  exc_df,
  "Leading 30 of 1.141 excluded candidate entries in the Central Asian source ledger, consolidated into primary settlements.",
  c("Candidate Site", "Country", "Classification", "Consolidation Method"),
  list(label = "tab:excluded-turan", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Archaeological Caveats and Taphonomic Preservation

Two primary taphonomic factors condition mediaeval settlement analysis across Central Asia [@Roberts2024Using; @Franklin2023Archaeolog]. First, the predominant use of unfired mudbrick (*pakhsa*) and rammed earth in monumental architecture makes ancient ruins highly susceptible to aeolian erosion, saline groundwater degradation and alluvial burial [@Roberts2024Using; @MirMakhamad2024Agricultur]. In desert deltas such as the Murghab and Lower Amu Darya, shifts in river channels and sand dune encroachment have buried entire settlement networks under metres of sand, preserving street layouts but rendering them invisible without aerial and satellite remote sensing [@Roberts2024Using; @Ilxomovna2026Reconstruc].

Second, continuous multi-millennial habitation at primary oasis hubs, notably Bukhara, Samarkand, Tashkent, Khujand and Andijan, has resulted in deep stratified cultural deposits (*tepe*) where modern and early modern urban infrastructure overlies mediaeval horizons [@Roberts2024Using; @Pardaev2019Design]. Extensive archaeological investigation has consequently been concentrated on abandoned cities (e.g. Merv, Otrar, Balasagun, Kunya-Urgench) where architectural ground plans remain accessible, whereas active cities require opportunistic salvage archaeology during civil engineering works [@Roberts2024Using; @Anon2024Buran; @MOLDAGALIYEVA2024Socio]. These taphonomic factors demonstrate the necessity of integrating multi-proxy spatial models to reconstruct complete demographic landscapes.
